Review of the National TB Control Programme 
*321. SHRI S.M. LALJAN BASHA: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have made some changes in the policies relating 
to the National TB Control Programme during the last six months; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is a fact that nodal TB hospitals like L.R.S. Institute of T.B. 
and Respiratory Diseases in Delhi have become noted for abandoning poor 
patients after preliminary medication; and 
(d) the steps taken to review and direct the L.R.S. Institute of T.B. and 
respiratory diseases and such other institutions to have responsible and humane 
attitude towards TB patients? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) and (b) No changes have been made in the 
policies relating to the National T.B. Control Programme during the last six 
months. 
(c) and (d) Based on scientific evidence, domiciliary treatment was 
established as a core principle for treatment of T.B. under the National T.B. 
Control Programme since 1962. In the current Revised National Control 
Programme (RNTCP), domiciliary treatment is given to T.B. patients under 
the direct supervision of a DOT provider, in accordance with the 
internationally recommended DOTS (Directly Observed Treatment Short 
Course) Strategy. Under the RNTCP, diagnostic and treatment services have 
been decentralized to Peripheral Health Institutions (PHIs) so as to improve 
access for communities and T.B. patients. Diagnostic Centres, also known as 
Designated Microscopy Centres, have been established in the general Health 
facilities. T.B. hospitals and health facilities of other sectors. After T.B. 
diagnosis has been established, patients are referred to the treating PHIs for 
categorization for treatment and registration under DOTS. It is the 
reponsibility of the health staff to retrieve T.B. patients who default while under 
treatment and to ensure they continue DOTS treatment. Thus 
19 

RAJYA SABHA [18 August, 2006] 
under the programme, TB patients are accorded the status of a VIP and the responsibility 
of successful treatment outcome is with the health system. These patients become non 
infectious within a few weeks of starting T.B. treatment. Thus hospitalization in T.B. 
hospitals, which leads to stigmatization, is not necessary. 
However when necessary, T.B. patients can be hospitalized in general hospitals for 
other diagnostic investigations and management. Special provision has been made under 
the Programme to provide T.B. treatment in hospitals using Prolongation Pouches. 
T.B, patients after being discharged from hospitals, continue to receive DOTS 
treatment and follow up sputum examination from the respective DOTS Centres till 
they complete TB treatment and thus they are not abandoned. 
The staff at all hospitals providing T.B. treatment are given training In RNTCP in 
order to ensure high quality standardized T.B. management as per internationally 
recommended DOTS strategy throughout the country. 
All components of the Programme, including T.B. diagnosis and treatment at 
Health Units of all levels including L.R.S. Institute of T.B. and Respiratory Diseases 
and such other institutions, are monitored and supervised based on the detailed 
Programme guidelines developed for this purpose so as to ensure quality of 
services. 
The performance of the programme in all PHIs including hospitals like LRS, Delhi, 
are reviewed based on their monthly and quarterly reports and necessary feedback is 
provided.

Eradication of leprosy 
†*325.  SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA: 
SHRI MOTILAL VORA: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government are making continuous efforts for eradication of 
leprosy from the country; 
(b) if so, the number of leprosy cases detected, so far, during the current 
year in the country, especially in Chhattisgarh; 
(c) the reasons for not eliminating leprosy completely from the States where 
there is much prevalence of leprosy; and 
(d) whether. Government would, with the help of concerned State 
Governments, make some special efforts for eradication of leprosy? 
THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
AMBUMANI RAM DOSS): (A) to (d) The goal set by National Health Policy, 
2002, was elimination of leprosy as a public health problem (i.e. prevalence 
rate of less than one case per ten thousand population) at National level by 
December, 2005. The goal of leprosy elimination at the national level was 
achieved as targeted in the month of December, 2005. Elimination has been 
achieved in 26 States/UTs. Now the programme is making efforts for achieving 
elimination in remaining States/UTs, which are: Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, 
Orissa, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal, Chandigarh, D&N Haveli and Delhi. The 
reasons for these States/UTs not having achieved elimination are- (i) 
Launching Multi Drug Therapy (MDT) late in all the districts due to poor 
health infrastructural facilities and (ii) problem of migration of population in 
Delhi, Chandigarh and Dadra Nagar Haveli. 
Special efforts are being made in all these areas with emphasis on 
situational analysis, specific measures for case detection and treatment, 
improved supervision, giving special focus to high endemic districts and blocks 
and strong IEC efforts to promote self  referral and adherence to treatment. 
These efforts are expected to lead to elimination of Leprosy in these nine 
States/UTs. 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
30 

[18 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
37426 new leprosy cases have been detected so far in the country in 
2006-07 as on 30th June, 2006, out of which 1700 (4.54%) leprosy cases are 
from Chhattisgarh State. 
The Government of India is committed to implementing the National 
Leprosy Elimination Compaign throughout the country even after 
achievement of elimination at the national level. These efforts are expected to 
lead to eradication of leprosy in the long term. 
NRHM in North Eastern Region 
*326. SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE: Will the Minister of 
HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) the progress, so far, made in carrying out of objectives of the 
National Rural Health Mission in the North Eastern Region, indicating the 
estimated population for whom health facilities are still beyong reach, State-
wise; 
(b) the allocation of Central funds for the mission during the current year 
and during the preceding three years, and the population and the area covered 
under the mission during each year, State-wise; and 
(c) the criteria adopted for allocation of Central funds for the mission and 
the steps taken to ensure the prevention of leakage, diversion or 
misappropriation of funds? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (A) The National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) 
has been launched on12th April, 2005, and is beign implemented throughout the 
country with special focus on 18 States which includes all the NE States (and 
Sikkim). It aims at providing integrated, comprehensive and effective primary 
health care to the poor, vulnerable sections of the society. 
State Health Missions have been constituted in all North Eastern States 
and Sikkim. The merger of Health & Family Welfare Departments in all the 
States have been completed and the State Health and Family Welfare 
Societies have been merged in all these States except in the State of Sikkim 
and 376 Rogi Kalyan Samitis have so far been registered. 15,629 ASH As have 
been selected so fare in Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Mizoram and 
Nagaland. 
31 

RAJYA SABHA [18 August, 2006] 
The RCH II, Janani Suraksha Yojana have also been launched in the NE 
States. There has been progress in various important programmes like the Blindness 
Control Programme, Routine Immunization etc. 
United Fund of Rs. 10,000/- has been released to each of the Sub Centres in 
the NE Region. 158 CHCs have been selected for upgradation as per the Indian Public 
Health Standards. During the Mission period (2005-2012), all the PHCs would be 
made fully functional on 24x7 basis. 
A North East division has been set up in the Ministry. A North Eastern Regional 
Resource Centre (NE-RRC) has also been set up at Guwahati with support from 
European Commission. The aim of NERRC is to provide technical assistance to the 
NE states and would work with these states to identify the core areas to be focused in 
the short, medium and long run and plan, for providing the missing technical and 
managerial capacity. 
One State Facilitator in each of the North Eastern States (including Sikkim) has 
been appointed to facilitate implementation of NRHM, recently, the Competent 
Authority has approved the detailed Framework for Implementation of National Rural 
Health Mission which inter-alia envisages relaxation of existing norms in favour of 
NE States in view of the special needs of these States. 
(b) During the year 2005-06, an amount of Rs. 325.73 Crore have been 
released to these States under NRHM. The detailed State-wise allocation of the 8 
NE States under NRHM for the year 2005-06 and 2006-07 is given in the 
Statement (See below). 
(c) The allocation of the funds to the States is on the basis of several parameters 
like population, prevalence of disease, State specific requirements, shortage of 
manpower and health infrastructure, etc. 
The NRHM provides for enhanced funding for various activities under the Mission 
and, therefore, detailed monitoring and accountability protocols have been ensured 
at all levels. Enhanced accountability is envisaged through community ownership 
and participation in management of health facilities and programmes, regular 
monitoring through data collection and building of accounting and managerial 
capacity at all levels. In addition, the Chartered Accountancy Firms have been engaged 
by NERRC to undertake finalization of accounts of all the 
32 

[18 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
8 NE States and several workshops have been conduced to streamline the 
financial management of these States. 
The funds are released to the states based upon submission of Statement 
of Expenditure (SOE) and Utilization Certificates in accordance with the 
guidelines of the Ministry of Finance. The expenditure of the states is 
auditable by the Accountant General and under the NRHM, Programme 
Management Units at State and District levels have been set up to implement

Recall system for hazardous foods 
*340. SHRI MAHENDRA MOHAN: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that recently a detailed scheme has been formulated to 
introduce a system for recall of hazardous foods from the market, if they are 
adulterated, misbranded or injurious to health; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the details of view expressed by various State Governments and machinery 
established or proposed for effective implementation of the recall system; and 
(d) the details of the recall system for hazardous foods as practiced in some other 
countries? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMADOSS): (a) to (d) The Joint Parliamentary Committee on 
Pesticide Residues in and safety standards for soft drinks, fruit juices and other beverages 
in its report submitted to Parliament on 04.2.2004 has recommended tor establishment of a 
mandatory recall system of food products. The relevant para of the report is reproduced 
below:— 
Para 4.78 (6)—A Mandatory Food Recall System should be established 
and companies should be made accountable for selling substandard and harmful 
products in the market which must be destroyed in the presence of authorities. 
Withdrawal notices must be issued in media to inform citizens so that they should 
be made aware about the unsafe products. In order to check adulteration in the food 
items, the Govemment should not hesitate in taking help of NGOs. The Government 
must also improve surveillance and monitoring the quality of the food. 
A draft notification to amend the Prevention of Food Adulteration (PFA) Rules, 
1955, to insert a provision for establishment of Food Recall System has been 
published in the Gazette of India vide GSR 355 (E) dated 09.6.2006 for inviting 
comments from the Public, giving 60 days time for sending comments, if any, on the 
draft rules from the date of its publication in the Official Gazette. 
 
49 

RAJYASABHA [18 August, 2006] 
As per the proposed provisions, no person shall himself or by any person 
on his behalf, manufacture for sale or store, sell distribute or exhibit for sale 
any article of food which is pre-packed, unless he has in place a system or 
procedure to recall the article of food or any ingredient or any substance placed in 
the market which is adulterated or misbranded or injurious to health. 
Before finalizing the proposed rules, the comments received on the draft 
proposed rules from the public, other countries, if any, would be considered 
alongwith the comments received from State/UT Governments who 
implement the PFA Act, 1954 and PFA Rules, 1955 in their respective 
States/UTs. No separate consultation with the States/ UTs undertaken. 
In the food regulations implemented by countries like Australia, New 
Zealand, Canada, countries of EU and USA, there are provisions for 
mentioning the details of Batch No., Code No. (Bar code, Matrix Code, Alfa 
numerical, Radio Frequency Identification etc.), complete address and other 
specific particulars of the manufacture on the label of food articles to 
facilitate product tracing and product recall.

2263. SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government would consider exploring the potential of 
Jatropha as the ideal feedstock for bio-diesel; 
59 

RAJYA SABHA [18 August, 2006] 
(b) whether Jatropha lends itself to all-climate conditions, has low gestation 
period and high seed yielding potential; 
(c) whether according to estimates, Jatropha cultivation on a mere 11 million 
hectares out of the country's total wasteland area of 63 million hectares has the potential to 
save around Rs. 20,000 crores on oil import bill; and 
(d) whether Government would launch a broad policy initiative on the large 
scale production of bio-feedstock based on Jatropha? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI 
KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) and (b) The Committee on Development of bio-fuels 
constituted by Planning Commission, submitted its report in July, 2003, which, inter-
alia, recommended large scale plantations of Jatropha on the wastelands for bio-diesel 
production. Jatropha lends itself to plantation with advantage, on land developed on 
watershed basis and on low fertility marginal, degraded, fallow, waste and other such 
lands. Jatropha has a gestation period of 2 years and it starts giving economic yield 
only after 4-5 years depending upon various agro-climatic factors. It has the potential to 
yield 2-3 MT/ha. under favourable conditions. 
(c) The Committee on Development of Bio-fuels has projected that the plantation 
of Jatropha on 11.19 million ha. of wastelands would provide feedstock for 
production of 13.38 million MT of bio-diesel for meeting the 20% blending 
requirement, which in-turn will help in reducing the huge oil import bill. 
(d) The draft National Policy on Bio-fuels formulated by Ministry of Non-
Conventional Energy Sources envisages utilization of wide range of crops including 
Jatropha for bio-diesel production.

Committee probing into the cause for suicides 
2266. SHRI M. V. MYSURA REDDY: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Committee appointed by the Prime Minister to probe the 
causes of growing farmers' suicides has submitted its report: 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the measures recommended to redress the alarming situation and the 
action proposed in the matter? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) to (c) No Committee has been appointed by 
the Prime Minister exclusively to probe the causes of growing suicide cases by 
farmers. At the instance of the Prime Minister's Office (PMO), a Fact Finding 
Team was constituted by the Planning Commission to, inter alia, find out the 
factors leading to rural di stress in the Vidarbha region of Maharashtra and to 
study the existing relief packages 
62 

[18 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
announced by the State Government, and to recommend necessary measures 
for addressing the issue of rural di stress. The Team has given various 
recommendation such as provisions for distribution of appropriate seeds, 
advisory and extension services, waiver of institutional credit, disciplining 
unlicensed money lenders, streamlining institutional credit flow, water 
harvesting and conservation, regional development plans, procurement and 
pricing, value addition of cotton, empowerment of farmer growers, setting up 
contributory fund and self help groups, and crop insurance. 
The Prime Minister alongwith Agriculture Minister visited the Vidarbha 
region of Maharashtra during 30th June to 1st July, 2006 and announced a 
detailed package of assistance to the affected districts which, inter alia, 
contains provision for ex-gratia assistance from the Prime Minister's National 
Relief Fund, debt relief to farmers, enhanced credit flow, interest waiver, assured 
irrigation facilities, seed replacement and cropping intensity, watershed 
development, horticulture development, micro irrigation, extension services, 
and subsidiary income opportunities. Actions are underway for 
implementation of the package. The PMO as well as Ministry of Agriculture 
is regularly reviewing the progress of implementation to ensure that the 
benefit of the announced package reaches the needy farmers fully and 
expeditiously. 
At the instance of the PMO, a Planning Commission team alongwith 
officials of the Government of Kerala visited Wayanad district of the State 
from 7th to 11th June, 2006, to study the problems pertaining to agricultural 
distress in the district and suggest remedial measures. The team submitted its 
report to the Planning Commission which is being examined.

Agro-Policy for rain fed area 
2278. SHRI C. PERUMAL: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have no agro-policy for the rain fed 
areas; 
(b) if so, whether there is any proposal to initiate an agro-policy for 60 per cent 
of rain fed agricultural lands; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI 
KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) to (c) The National Agricultural Policy 2000 addresses 
issues of sustainable agriculture which include watershed development in rainfed 
areas. As per this policy integrated and holistic development of rainfed areas has been 
given emphasis through conservation of rainwater by vegetative measures on watershed 
basis and augmentation of biomas production through agro and farm forestry with the 
involvement of the watershed community. The policy document also envisages a long 
term prospective plan for sustainable rainfed agriculture through watershed approach for 
development of two third of India's cropped area which is dependant on rains.

National Crop Forecasting Centres 
2280. SHRI VARINDER SINGH BAJWA: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Govemment have set up the National Crop Forecasting Centre; 
(b) if so, the main purpose and function of the centre; and 
(c) the extent to which it has been proved beneficial to farming community? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI 
KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) The scheme of National Crop Forecasting Centre (NCFC) was approved 
with the objective of providing an effective unified institutional framework for 
entire crop forecasting system in the country involving data flow from diverse channels 
for getting more accurate crop production estimates. The NCFC started functioning 
with effect from 3rd December, 1998. 
The NCFC is mainly involved in coordinating the activities under the scheme 
"Forecasting of Agricultural output using Space, Agro-meteorology and Land 
based observations (FASAL). Further, NCFC also coordinates the activities under the 
project" Development of Extended Range Forecast System (ERFS) for Climate Risk 
Management in Agriculture" and holds meetings of the multi-disciplinary Crop 
Weather Watch Group (CWWG) every week to review the weather and crop 
situation, among others. The CWWG provides an effective institutional mechanism 
facilitating crucial inputs for tracking crop prospects and that of early warning.

urban areas. 
The schemes relating to khadi are implemented through khadi institutions 
affiliated with the KVIC/Khadi and Village Industries Boards of States/Union 
Territories. Khadi is mainly an agro-based activity. 
The Government implements a number of schemes for development of the coir 
industry, in coconut growing States, through the Coir Board. 
(d) Applications for setting up industry units mentioned at (a) above are not 
received directly by the Government in the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries. Under 
REGP, an eligible entrepreneur can establish a village industry by availing of margin 
money assistance from KVIC and loans from any public sector scheduled 
commercial bank. For this purpose, the prosepctive entrepreneur has to submit a 
project proposal to the State offices of KVIC or the District offices of the respective State/ 
Union Territory Khadi and Village Industries Board (KVIB) or the implementing 
banks directly. Approval of the project depends on technical and financial appraisal by the 
respective banks. Similarly, under PMRY, an eligible educated unemployed youth can 
establish a self-employment unit of village industry in the rural areas by availing of 
permissible subsidy and loan from the banks. This Yojana is implementing through the 
District Industries Centres of States and Union Territories. For this purpose, the 
prospective entrepreneur has to submit a project proposal to the District Industries 
Centre concerned, which in turn, sponsors short-listed applications to the 
implementing banks.

Medicines at reasonable prices 
2291. DR. (SHRIMATI) NAJMA A. HEPTULLA: Will the Minister of 
CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) the mechanism in place to regulate/control the prices of various categories of 
medicines; 
(b) the details for each category thereof; 
(c) the steps taken/proposed to ensure that the selling price of a medicine is not 
exorbitant when compared with its intrinsic value; and 
(d) how Govemment propose to ensure that the medicines which are to be taken 
life long are priced reasonably and the manufacturers/ traders do not indulge in 
undue profiteering? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS AND 
FERTILIZERS (SHRI B.K. HANDIQUE): (a) to (d) The objectives of the 
Pharmaceutical Policy include, inter alia ensuring abundant availability at reasonable 
prices within the country of good quality essential pharmaceuticals of mass 
consumption. 
As per the present Pharma Pricing Policy, the 74 bulk drugs specified in the First 
Schedule of the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 1995 (DPCO. 95) and the formulations 
based thereon are under price control and their prices are fixed/revised by the National 
Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) in accordance with the provisions of the DPCO, 
95. These drugs have been kept under price control on the basis of criteria mentioned in 
'Modifications in Drug Policy, 1986', announced in September, 1994. 
Prices of non-Scheduled formulations are fixed by the manufacturers themselves 
keeping in view the various factors like cost of production, marketing expenses, 
R&D expenses, trade commission, market 
97 

RAJYA SABHA [18 August, 2006] 
competition, product innovation, product quality etc., The NPPA monitors the 
prices of medicines as per monthly Retail Audit Reports of ORG-IMS 
Research Pvt. Ltd. The Govemment takes corrective measures where the 
public interest is found to be adversely affected. 
A Draft National Pharmaceutical Policy, 2006 has been prepared. The 
Policy proposes, inter alia, limits for trade margin on medicines. Special 
attention is being given to the prices of medicines, which are required on a life 
long basis so as to make their prices reasonable. After the finalization of the 
Cabinet note on the Policy, it would be placed before the Cabinet for 
approval.

geographical or correspondence address to consumers;

companies where they can personally go and lodge their consumer grievances; 
 
(c) whether Government have taken steps to ensure that all companies give 
their actual addresses, phone numbers and other such details; 
(d) to what extent companies have been hiding behind call centres to avoid any 
direct interaction with customers; and

addresses? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, 
FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI TASLIMUDDIN): (a) to (e) The 
Companies Act, 1956 provides for declaration of addresses by a company in its business 
transactions. Section 147 of the Companies Act, 1956 provides, inter-alia, that every 
company shall have its name and the address of its registered office mentioned in 
legible characters in all its business letters, in all its bill heads and letter paper, and in all its 
notices and other official publications and also have its name so mentioned in 
all bills of exchange, hundies, promissory notes, endorsements, cheques and 
orders for money or goods purporting to be signed by or on behalf of the company, 
and in all bills of parcels, invoices, receipts and letters of credit of the company. 
Besides, the Standards of Weights and Measures (Packaged Commodities) 
Rules 1977 provide that every package kept, offered or exposed for sale or sold, shall 
bear conspicuously on the package, the name and complete address of the 
manufacturer or where the manufacturer is not the packer, the name and address of the 
manufacturer and the packer. After a recent amendment to these Rules, every package is 
required to bear the name, address, telephone number, E-mail address,

2321. DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) what are the genesis and objectives of National River 
Conservation Programme and National Lake Conservation Programme; 
(b) whether any financial assistance has been granted to Rajasthan, under 
NRCP and NLCP, for rejuvenation/reclamation of certain historically and 
environmentally important rivers and lakes; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; 
(d) If not, the reasons therefor; 
(e) whether any proposal from Rajasthan, are pending with the Central 
Government in above context; and 
(f) if so, the details thereof and the Centre's reaction thereto? 
130 

[18 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORMESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) The work of 
pollution abatement of rivers started with the launching of Ganga Action 
Plan(GAP) Phase-I in the year 1985. Subsequently, GAP Phase-ll was 
initiated, which included the works on the tributaries of river Ganga namely, 
Yamuna, Gomti and Damodar. The plan was further broad based to cover 
polluted stretches of other major rivers in the country under the aegis of the 
National River Conservation Plan (NRCP) in the year 1995. The objective of 
NRCP is to improve the water quality in these rivers, which are a major 
source of fresh water in the country through the implementation of various 
pollution abatement schemes. 
The National Lake Conservation Plan (NLCP) has been initiated in 2001 
with the objective to restore and conserve polluted and degraded lakes of the 
country. The thrush under the Plan is to undertake in situ lake remediation 
measures like de-weeding, de-silting, bio-remediation, etc. together with works 
like interception, diversion and treatment of sewage discharge into the lake 
and lake front development. 
(b) to (d) Under the NRCP, four schemes pertaining to interception, 
diversion and treatment of sewage, low cost sanitation, river front 
development and improved wood crematoria have been sanctioned for 
Keshoraipatan and three schemes pertaining to low cost sanitation, river front 
development and improved wood crematoria have been sanctioned for Kota 
in Rajasthan for abatement of pollution of river Chambal. The total 
sanctioned cost of these seven schemes is Rs. 1.17 crore, against which Rs. 
1.12 crore has been released till date for their implementation. 
Under the NLCP, the project for revival/rejuvenation of Mansagar Lake 
stands sanctioned for Rs. 24.72 crore. The works to be taken up under the 
project include realignment of drains, construction of sewage treatment plant, 
desilting, in situ biological treatment of lake water body, construction of 
wetlands, afforestation of lake catchment area, etc. The project is being 
implemented on 70:30 cost sharing pattern between Government of India and 
the State Government, and funds amounting to Rs. 15 crore have been 
released till date as Government of India's share for the project

AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that as per the survey conducted by the Central 
Pollution Control Board, Godavari-from Polavaram to Rajahmundry, 
Nagavalli from Nagavalli to Thotapalli and Musi between Hyderabad and 
Secundrabad stretch are among very polluted rivers in Andhra Pradesh; 
137 

RAJYA SABHA [18 August, 2006] 
(b) if so, the source of pollution of these rivers and the main factors 
responsible for pollution in these rivers; and 
(c) the details of efforts made, so far/proposed to be made by 
Government to make these rivers clean and check the pollution in these rivers? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) As per the survey 
conducted by the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) alongwith Andhra 
Pradesh Pollution Control Board (APPCB), river Godavari is polluted in the 
stretch from Polavaram to Rajahmundry, river Nagavalli along Thotapalli 
Regulator and river Musi downstream of Hyderabad, and are having Bio-
chemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) values ranging between 6 to 44mg/1. 
(b) These rivers are polluted by the discharge of municipal and industrial 
wastewater. Inadequate flow of fresh water is also responsible for deterioration

fifteen industrial units discharging wastewater into the rivers of Godavari and

2327. SHRI EKANATH K. THAKUR: Will the Minister of

crops may have human and economic cost; 
138

(b) whether it is also a fact that the Bt. gene in GM crops has been found 
to be toxic and Coalition for GM Free India (CFGMFI) have established that 
Bt. gene affects human and livestock health adversely; and 
(c) if so, when Japan and several European countries have banned 
cultivation of GM food crops, the reasons for allowing its entry without 
taking adequate precautions? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) Introduction of any 
new technology may have both beneficial and adverse impacts and requires 
careful evaluation of the long term sustainable benefits. The Government of 
India is following a policy of case by case approval process for transgenic 
crops. The product is approved for environmental release only when there is a 
clear socio-economic and technical justification for release of the product. 
(b) GM crops having Bt. gene are being consumed in several countries 
and there was no scientific evidence generated either by CFGMFI or any 
other organization on toxicity of Bt. gene to human and animal health. All 
genetically modified food is tested for toxicity and allergenicity prior to its 
approval for human consumption. 
(c) Japan and European countries consumes GM food crops and some of 
the countries like Spain, France, Germany do cultivate GM crops. Bt. Cotton 
is the only transgenic crop approved for commercial cultivation in lndia. No 
GM food crop has been permitted for commercial cultivation or marketing in 
India.

Primary census data of Tigers 
2329. SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that 15 out of 17 tiger States have failed to file their primary 
census data with regard to tiger population; 
(b) if so, which States have filed their census data, and which ones have not yet 
filed the same and the details of the tiger population, as posted, in each State; and 
(c) whether any dependable and effective way has been found or evolved for 
arriving at accurate and correct population of tigers? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA):(a) and (b) Phase-I data pertaining to the All 
India tiger Estimation, using the refined methodology, has been received from 15 States, 
which include Andhra Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, 
Karnataka, Kerala, Mizoram, Orissa, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal, Jharkhand and Uttaranchal. 
Phase-I data has not been received so far from Rajasthan and Maharashtra. The 
Phase-I data provides information only on the presence and relative abundance of tigers. The 
population estimation of tiger requires further sampling followed by analysis (Phases II & 
III). 
(c) The refined methodology of estimating tigers involves sampling and estimation 
of tiger density in different strata using a combination of methods, i.e. camera trap, digital 
photography of pugmarks to fix identities by a computer based recognition technique 
based on a mark-capture statistical framework, and correlation with other data, e.g. 
physical signs of tiger presence, prey-base, apart from DNA characterization of scats at 
places. The methodology has been approved by the Tiger Task Force constituted by 
National Board for Wildlife. The process involves three phases and its Phase-I alone 
has been completed and the latest estimation figures would be known after 
completion of Phase-lll of the process.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND

Flu from M/s. Roche. Another 7,00,000 capsules of Oseltamivir Phpsphate 
(generic version of Tami Flu) have been procured from Hetero Drugs, an Indian

its stockpile. For chemoprophylaxis of high' risk personnel and treatment of suspected

drug is necessary for chemoprophylaxis of contacts of cases and personnel involved in 
culling, clean up, rapid response, surveillance, who are all categorized as high risk 
personnel. The drug is also required for treatment of human cases of Avian Influenza 
and pandemic influenza. The available stock may have to be utilized if a need arises to 
contain outbreaks in future. This drug has a self life of 3 to 5 years.

SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) how does Government define an epidemic; 
(b) the details of number of epidemic outbreaks in" last five years alongwith 
annual fatalities in epidemics, year-wise; 
145 

RAJYA SABHA [18 August, 2006] 
(c) the names of the regions that have been affected by the epidemic outbreak; 
(d) the details of the epidemic surveillance network in the country and the steps 
required to strengthen the network; 
(e) what steps are taken to strengthen the public health system to minimize the 
outbreak of epidemics; and 
(f) which are the agencies involved in epidemic surveillance, and control 
network and how is their performance monitored? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) An epidemic is defined as the 
unusual occurrence of a disease, specific health related behaviour or other health-related 
events in a community or region, clearly in excess of expected occurrence. 
(b) and (c) A list of outbreaks investigated by National Institute of 
Communicable Diseases for the period from 2001-2005 is given in the Statement (see 
below). 
(d) to (f) Health is primarily a State subject and the State Governments are required to 
take necessary action for effective surveillance, early detection and quick response 
to epidemic outbreaks. The Union Government supplements the efforts of the 
State Government by providing technical guidance and other inputs. 
For effective surveillance and early detection of epidemic outreaks, National 
Surveillance Programme for Communicable Diseases (NSPCD) was implemented in 101 
districts of the country, which has been replaced by a comprehensive programme 
Integrated Diseases Surveillance Project (I DSP) in November, 2004. IDSP will 
cover all districts of the country by 2006-07 in a phased manner. The objective of 
IDSP is to establish a decentralized State based system of surveillance for 
communicable and non-communicable diseases so that timely and effective public 
health action can be initiated in response to health challenges in the country. The 
project is receiving technical assistance from several partners and stakeholders 
includding National technical institutions like Indian Council of Medical Research 
(ICMR), National Institute of Communicable Diseases (NICD), Central Bureau of 
Health Intelligence (CBHI) etc.

functioning of CGHS and if so, the mandate of the Committee; 
(d) if so, whether the Committee has submitted its report; 
(e) if so, the details of its recommendations; and 
(f) if not, the reasons for delay in submitted the report?

FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) and (b) No, 
Sir, against sanctioned strength of 1676 posts in GDMO and non-teaching 
specialist doctors sub-cadre of Central Health Service, 198 clear vacancies 
exist at present. Requisitions have been sent to UPSC for filling up these 
vacant posts; 
(c) Yes, Sir. Terms of the Reference of the Committee is given in the 
Statement (See below). 
(d) No, Sir. 
(e) and (f) The Committee has so far held 12 meetings and on the 
suggestions of the Committee during the deliberations the following 
measures have been initiated:— 
(i) Computerisations of CGHS dispensaries at Laxmi Nagar Delhi as a 
pilot project has been running successfully. Installation of computer 
hardware, data entry, and internet connectivity has been completed in the 
CGHS dispensaries in North Avenue, South Avenue and Parliament 
Annexe. Computerisation of CGHS dispensaries in Delhi has also been 
taken up in remaining CGHS dispensaries.

dispensaries comprising of th e CMO in-charge, Area Welfare 
Officers and representatives of beneficiaries to consider various 
grievances of beneficiaries and also try to make local level 
improvements in the functioning of the dispensaries. 
(iii) As recommended by Kaul Committee more powers have been 
delegated to Zonal Additional Directors to decentralize the 
functioning of CGHS, Medical reimbursement claims and bills of local

ORDER    
Subject: Setting up of a Committee under the Chairmanship of Shri P.K. Kaul 
to review the functioning of the CGHS and forgiving recommendations 
for making it more user-friendly-regarding— 
The undersigned is directed to state that the matter regarding review of the 
functioning of CGHS has been drawing the attention of the Govt, for some 
time past. It has now been decided to constitute a Committee under the 
Chairmanship of Shri P.K. Kaul to review the functioning of the CGHS and 
for giving recommendations for making it more user-friendly. The members 
of the Committee would be as under:— 
(i) Shri P.K. Kaul, former Cabinet Secretary Chairman 
(ii) Shri Javed A. Chaudhary, former Health Secretary        Member 
(iii) Dr. S.P.Agarwal, DG (Health Services) Member 
158 

[18 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
(iv) Joint Secretary in the Department of Health Member 
dealing with CGHS 
v) Dr. P.K. Phukan, Director, CGHS Member Secretary 
2. The Committee shall look into the functioning of the CGHS scheme and 
make recommendations for making it more user-friendly. Some of the 
illustrative areas that may be looked into include:— 
(i) Availability/shortage of medicines (including life saving medicines) in 
the CGHS dispensaries. 
(ii) Delay in the supply of indented Medicines to the CGHS beneficiaries 
through the CGHS authorized local chemists. 
(iii) Quality of medicines, spurious/substandard supplied to the 
beneficiaries. 
(iv) Substitution of medicines with a different brand name medicine by the 
CGHS authorized local chemist, Grievance of beneficiaries due to 
non-availability of CGHS authorized local chemist for the particular 
dispensary, and inconvenience caused to the CGHS beneficiaries due to 
Strike by the CGHS authorized local chemists. 
(v) Pending madical claims of CGHS beneficiaries resulting in delay in the 
reimbursement of medical expenses to the beneficiaries. 
(vi) Availability of Specialist OPD consultation for the CGHS 
beneficiaries. 
(vii) Quality of diagnostic/pathology services given by the CGHS 
laboratories/CGHS Polyclinic to the beneficiaries. 
(viii) Quality of Indoor (IPD) services and diagnostic/investigation facilities 
given to the CGHS beneficiaries at the CGHS recognized private 
hospitals and at the Central Government/State Government hospitals 
and Institutions. 
(ix) Punctuality/behaviour of the CGHS doctors and staff at the CGHS 
dispensaries towards the beneficiaries, Cleanliness and availability of 
the basic minimum infrastructure and equipment in the CGHS 
dispensaries. 
159 

RAJYA SABHA [18 August, 2006] 
(x) Ratio of Patients vis-a-vis Doctor (including support staff) keeping in view the 
average monthly attendance in the various dispensaries. 
(xi) Suggest measures to reduce/stop misuse of CGHS facility. 
3. The Committee will also look into and suggest changes with 
respect to the financial viability of the scheme in view of the rapidly 
increasing expenditure in CGHS. The Committee may suggest alternative 
cost effective models of healthcare provisioning to Government 
employees as well as alternative sources of financing the CGHS. The 
Committee may also suggest changes in the following:— 
(i) Monthly CGHS contribution rates to make the CGHS scheme more viable. 
(ii) Converting the CGHS organization, a Subordinate Office under the Directorate 
General of Health Services, into a Corporation on the lines of the Employees State 
Insurance Corporation (ESIC).

thereof; and 
(f) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI):(a) to (f) Government of India 
announced the National Policy on Older Persons (NPOP) in 1999. 
Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment is the nodal agency for 
implementation of the National Policy for older persons. The NPOP provides for the 
following to fulfil its objectives: 
1. Financial security through old age pension scheme for poor and destitute 
elderly, creating opportunities for skill upgradation, continued education and 
self employment, better return on savings and higher rebate in tax and 
concessional fare for the elderly. 
2. Health security by strengthening and reorienting services at primary health 
care level, promoting the creation of health facilities through NGOs, 
implementing insurance linked health scheme. 
3. Recognising shelter as basic human need earmarking houses/ housing site for the 
elderly belonging to lower income groups special consideration under schemes like 
Indira Awas Yojana for elderly in the category of BPL, loans at resonable 
interest etc. 
4. Education. 
5. Welfare & Institutional care. 
6. Legal safeguards -protection of life and property. 
7. Taining of manpower. 
8. Media-to identify emerging issues and area of action and promoting 
inter generational bonds.

2339. SHRI ABU ASIM AZMI: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND

FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI):(a) to (d) The 
Government has decided to support the Public Health Foundation of India (PHFI) 
in setting up world class Institutes of Public Health in India. PHFI is an 
autonomous Public-Private partnership wherein the Government of India proposes 
to continue as one time grant upto Rs. 65 crore to the initial Rs. 200 crore PHFI

public health management. It will not only train health

public health would be able to trian more than 2000 public health professionals 
annually, in addition to turning out 150 Masters of public Health per year.

TB and AIDS 
2344. SHRI S. ANBALAGAN: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of persons affected by Tuberculosis (TB) and number of 
them died during each of the last three years, State-wise; 
(b) the steps being taken/proposed to be taken by Government to totally 
eliminate this disease; 
(c) whether it is a fact that AIDS and TB form a lethal combination; and 
167 

RAJYA SABHA [18 August, 2006] 
(d) if so, the details thereof and the steps proposed to be taken in this 
regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) It is 
estimated that every year about 18 lakh new cases are occurring in the country 
of which approximately 8 lakh are new sm ear positive and, therefore, highly 
infectious. State-wise detail of patients detected and put on treatment during 
last three years under the Revised National TB Control Programme (RNTCP) 
is given at Statement-I (See below). It is estimated that about 3.7 lakh persons 
die of TB every year in the country. Deaths were not reported under the 
National TB Control Programme which was being implemented in the country 
prior to the launch of RNTCP. However, under the Revised National TB Control 
Programme (RNTCP), deaths due to TB among patients registered for treatment 
are reported. State-wise details of deaths during the last 3 years are given in 
the Statement-Il (See below). 
(b) To control TB, the Revised National TB Control Programme 
(RNTCP) widely known as DOTS, which is WHO recommended strategy, is 
being implemented as a 100% Centrally Sponsored Scheme from 1997 in the 
country in a phased manner. Its objective is to achieve cure rate of 85% of new 
sputum positive cases and to detect at least 70% of such cases. By March 23, 
2006, all the districts in the country have been brought under coverage and are 
implementing RNTCP. Under the programme, diagnosis and treatment 
facilities including supply of anti TB drugs are provided free of cost to all TB 
patients. 
(c) Yes, Sir. 
(d) TB is most common opportunistic infection in the HIV infected 
individuals. An HIV infected individual co-infected with TB bacilli has an 
annual 10% risk of developing active TB disease, as compared to 10% lifetime 
risk of developing active TB disease in HIV negative individuals. Also TB 
disease is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in people living with 
HlV/AIDS. 
To address the problem, a close coordination has been established between 
the Revised National TB Control Programme (RNTCP) and the National 
AIDS Control Programme, at the National, State and district level so as to 
ensure that HIV positive individuals have early access to 
168 

[18 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
RNTCP diagnostic and treatment services and TB patients being treated under 
RNTCP who are infected with HIV have optimal access to care and support 
for HIV disease.

PHCs in Rajasthan 
2355. DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of Primary Health Centres functioning in Rajasthan; 
(b) whether these Centres are adequate to meet the need of general public 
as per national norms and population; 
(c) whether these PHCs have basic infrastructure to deal with the general 
and specialised requirements of the patients; 
(d) whether Government propose to open new PHCs, in near future, and 
(e) if so, the details thereof and what would be the contribution of the 
Central Government? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) A total of 
1713 Primay Health Centres [PHC] are functioning in Rajasthan. 
(b) As per block level population norms, [2001 census], there is a 
shortfall of 179 Primary Health Centres in Rajasthan State. 
(c) There is a shortage of 204 Primary Health Centres with buildings. 
(d) and (e) Yes, Sir. During the current financial year 22 PHCs are likely 
to be opened under the State Plan out of which sanction for 3 PHCs have 
been issued. As the PHCs would be opened under State Plan, so no Central 
Government contribution has been sought. 
Availability of beds in AIIMS 
2356. SHRI MOTIUR RAHMAN: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether due to lack of bed availability, AIIMS is not admitting 
seriously injured and ill persons; 
(b) if so, the steps taken to reserve beds especially for the seriously injured 
and ill persons; 
194 

[18 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) the total number of beds as on date and whether there is any proposal 
to increase their numbers and if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) the steps proposed to be taken to improve the quality of medical care in 
Safdarjung Hospital to reduce the load of AIIMS? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) and (b) In 
the Casualty/Emergency life saving situations all efforts are made to admit 
the seriously ill and injured patients. In case of non-availability of beds, such 
patients are accommodated in the other beds available in the Hospital. 
However, in case of even non-availability of other beds, patients are 
normally referred to other Government Hospitals for admission and 
continuation of treatment through AIIMS Ambulance 
(c) As on 30.04.2006, the sanctioned bed strength at AIIMS is 1995. The 
increase in bed strength is a continuous ongoing process and depend upon patient 
load, availability of resources, etc. 
(d) While steps are taken to upgrade the infrastructural facilities at 
Safdarjung Hospital, the Government has also drawn up the Pradhan Mantri 
Swasthya Suraksha Yojana (PMSSY), for setting up six Super Specialty 
AIIMS like Institutions in under-served areas with a view to reducing patient 
load, as substantial number of patients at AIIMS come from these under-served 
States. It is also proposed to upgrade some of the existing Government 
Medical Colleges/Institutions to the level of AIIMS.

Negotiations with World Bank for funding of RCH-I Project 
2359. SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state. 
(a) whether the Reproductive and Child Health-I Project which is an 
197 

RAJYA SABHA [18 August, 2006] 
important component of the National Rural Health Mission, has been 
submitted to the World Bank for approval; 
(b) if so, the details of the proposal and the decisions taken by the World 
Bank in this regard; 
(c) whether any negotiations with the World Bank have been held in 
connection with the funding to the said project; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; 
(e) whether RCH-I has since been closed on 30th September, 2004; and 
(f) if so, what alternative arrangements Government have made since 
September, 2004 to run this programme? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) Support of 
the World Bank has been sought for the Reproductive and Child Health phase 
two Programme (RCH-II) 
(b) The Government of India (GOI) and the Pooling Partners including the 
World Bank have agreed to a common design of the Programme with the 
following salient features: 
(1) Adoption of a sector wide approach so as to encompass within RCH-
II all the related reproductive, child and maternal health initiatives of 
the Govemment of lndia; 
(2) Decentralization of the programme design to enable each State and in 
due course each District to formulate its own need based Programme 
Implementation Plans (PIPs) following agreed parameters; 
(3) Flexible programming wherein each state is provided with an annual 
financial envelope to formulate and implement it's PIP; 
(4) Capacity building to strengthen the programme management 
capabilities at the State and District levels including establishment of 
programme Management Units to facilitate decentralization and need 
based planning; 
(5) Results Based Management with a focus on agreed outcome 
198 

[18 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
documented in individual MoU's between the Gol and the State/ UTs 
and a Pro-poor focus with a view to providing special attention to the 
primary health care needs of the vulnerable groups, particularly the 
SC/ST population; 
(6) Monitoring and Evaluation through a regular reporting system, 
external evaluation and community based monitoring systems; 
(7) Pool financing by Development Partners including the World Bank by 
contributing to the Programme Budget of the Gol instead of 
maintaining separate project budget and systems. 
(c) and (d) Yes Sir, the Government of India and the World bank, DFID 
and UNFPA undertook negotiations on the project from 12-15 July, 2006 to 
finalise the programme design and funding support. 
(e) and (f) The World Bank support to the first phase of the 
Reproductive and Child Health Project (RCH-I) ended on 30th September, 
2004. However, from October 2004 until end of the project i.e. 31st March, 
2005, the project continued with the help of domestic budgetary support. 
Thereafter since April 2005 the second phase of the Programme i.e. RCH-II has 
also similarly been continuing with domestic budgetary support pending 
finalization of World Bank funding.

Recommendations of study group on development of SSI 
2406. SHRI S.P.M. SYED KHAN: Will the Minister of SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that most of the recommendations of the study 
group on the development of small enterprises have been ignored and only a 
few of them have been implemented; and 
(b) the details of recommendations yet to be implemented and 
implemented, so far? 
THE MINISTER OF SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES (SHRI MAHABIR 
PRASAD): (a) and (b) Out of the 64 recommendations of the Study Group 
constituted under the chairmanship of Dr. S.P. Gupta, by the Planning 
Commission, 57 recommendations were accepted by the Government. The 
accepted recommendations yet to be implemented include enactment of laws 
relating to Limited Liability Partnerships and Factories Services as well as 
Simplification of Regulatory Laws. Action has been completed in respect of 
most of the other accepted recommendations, which, inter alia, include 
enhancement of excise exemption limit from Rs. 50 lakh to Rs. 1 crore, 
notification of the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 
2006 which provides for 3-tier definition of enterprises, covering micro, small 
and medium enterprises, setting up a cell in the office of Development 
Commissioner (Small Scale Industries) in  respect of matters relating to 
World Trade Organisation agreements, subsidy for technology upgradation 
(15% capital subsidy provided under Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme 
for technology upgradation), taking decisions on de-reservation of items 
reserved for exclusive manufacture by small scale industries (SSI) in 
consultation with the stakeholders, enhancement of investment ceiling for 
small manufacturing enterprises from Rs. 1 crore to Rs. 5 crore, conduct of 
fresh census for SSI sector, involvement of SSI Associations in census and 
other data collection, programme to modernize export-oriented industrial 
clusters, continuation of ISO 9000 certification scheme, specialized bank 
branches for SSI lending, etc.

Non-SSI units manufacturing items reserved for SSIs 
2408. SHRI T.T.V. DHINAKARAN: Will the Minister of SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that non-SSI units are permitted to manufacture 
items reserved for the SSI units under an obligation to export at least 50 
per cent of the production; 
(b) if so, the total production of reserved items by non-SSI units during 
the last three years; and 
(c) what penalty is imposed in case of non-export of 50 per cent of 
production as undertaken? 
THE MINISTER OF SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES (SHRI MAHABIR 
PRASAD): (a) Yes, Sir. Non-SSI units are permitted to manufacture items 
reserved for the SSI units subject to the condition that every such unit obtains 
an industrial licence issued by the Department of Industrial Policy and 
Promotion, Ministry of Commerce and Industry, with an obligation to export 
a minimum of 50% of the annual production to be achieved within a 
maximum period of 3 years. Such non-SSI units required to execute Legal 
Undertakings (LUT) with the Directorate General of Foreign Trade which 
monitors the fulfilment of export obligation. 
(b) The figures of production of reserved items by non-SSI units are not 
maintained centrally by the Government. 
(c) Non-fulfilment of the export obligation by such units is treated as a 
violation of the conditions incorporated in the industrial licence for which 
section 24 of the Industries (Development & Regulations) Act, 1951 provides 
for penalties. In addition, in the event of non-fulfilment of export obligation, 
the non-SSI unit concerned, on the instructions of the Government of India, is 
obliged to handover the manufactured goods to the extent of shortfall in 
fulfilment of the export obligation, to any agency that the Government may 
nominate for disposal in any manner. The amount recovered from such 
disposal of the goods is deposited with the 
253 

RAJYA SABHA [18 August, 2006] 
Government towards fulfilment of the export obligation condition. The 
defaulting unit is also liable to other action including the initiation of legal 
proceedings for confiscation of goods to the extent of shortfall in the 
obligation and refusal for further approval and or other liabilities, penalties 
and consequences under the provisions of Foreign Trade (Development and 
Regulation) Act, 1992 and the orders and rules made thereunder, as may be 
decided by the Government.

Captive iron-ore mines for steel makers 
2410. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of STEEL be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Hoda Committee in its draft report said that 
steel makers do not require captive iron-ore mines; 
(b) whether it is a fact that some of the steel makers has opposed the idea; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) the action Government propose to take in this matter? 
THE   MINISTER OF STATE   IN   THE MINISTRY   OF STEEL (DR. 
AKHILESH DAS): (a) No, Sir. Statement in annexed (see below), (b) to (d) In 
view of (a) above, does not arise. 
Statement 
Brief of Recommendations of Hoda Committee on Allocation of  
Captive Mines to Steel Makers 
• Stand-alone mining and captive mining should continue to coexist in 
the country. In 2016-17 the position should be reviewed in light of the 
emerging situation of establishment of steel capacity in the country on 
the one hand and accretions to the level of iron ore resources in the 
country, on the other. A view can be taken at that time if the balance of 
advantage in grant of LAPL/PL/ML should be changed in favour of 
steel mills. 
• In a situation of multiple applications for grant of iron ore LAPL/PL/ 
255 

RAJYASABHA [18 August, 2006] 
ML the existing investment in steel plants which have exhausted their 
current captive mines should also be a consideration. 
• Existing captive mines should be renewed if they have complied with 
the conditions of the lease and the life of the steel plant so warrants 
taking into account existing and planned capacities. 
• Steel making capacities already in existence on July 1, 2006, which 
do not have captive mines, may also be given preferential allocation of 
adequate iron ore reserves within the St3te without the need to go 
through the process of auction, as a one-time measure to provide a 
level playing field. 
• Scientific and vigorous prospecting in the country should be 
encouraged. LAPLs and PLs for magnetite may be freely given to 
both stand alone and captive miners whether Indian or foreign LAPLs 
for hematite may be given only after strictly ensuring that GSI or 
another state agency has not already done the requisite exploration. 
• Captive iron ore mines allotted to steel makers should use the ore 
from these mines for their own steel and should not sell the same 
either in India or abroad.

Status of Iron-ore mines in Jharkhand 
2412. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Will the Minister of STEEL be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Jharkhand Government has raised doubts 
of SAIL's ownership of iron-ore mines in the State; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) if SAIL's mining leases for iron-ores in Jharkhand are terminated or are 
not extended, what alternatives are available to it to ensure optimum level of 
production? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STEEL (DR. 
AKHILESH DAS): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b)After amalgamation of Indian Iron & Steel Company Limited (IISCO) 
with Steel Authority of India Limited (SAIL) w.e.f. 16th February, 2006, all the 
concerned department of Jharkhand Government were informed about the 
amalgamation order issued by the Department of Company Affairs, 
Government of India. However, the District Mining Officer, Chaibasa, 
Jharkhand issued a show cause notice to General Manager, IISCO Ltd. 
Gua/Manoharpur and SAIL on 6th July, 2006 for giving the control of Iron 
ore leases at Gua & Chiria to SAIL in illegal manner and without prior 
approval of State Government in violation to rule 37/46 of mineral 
concessions rules 1960 and also the terms and conditions of the leases' 
agreement. 
SAIL has contested this, mentioning that as per the lease agreement, the 
Lessee included the lease holder and also its successor. As such, the 
amalgamation does not violate any rule. Citing the fact of the lease agreement, 
the provisions in the scheme of amalgamation, approval of Board for 
Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR), approval of Government of 
India, Ministry of Steel and approval/order passed by Department of 
Company Affairs, Government of India, reply to show cause notice has been 
submitted on 13th July, 2006 to the District Mining Officer, Chaibasa, 
Jharkhand. 
(c) If SAIL's mining leases for iron ores in Jharkhand are terminated or are not 
extended in favour of SAIL, then it would be difficult for SAIL to continue 
optimum production & it will fail to achieve its growth plan as envisaged in its 
corporate plan 2011-12. The integrated Steel Plant of SAIL as Burnpur & Bokaro 
will be affected immediately and after a few years, other integrated Steel Plants in 
the eastern part of India will also get affected because of very limited reserves in 
other mines of SAIL in Orissa region.

GOVERNMENT BILL 
The Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Bill, 2005 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI A. RAJA): 
Sir. I beg to move" 
"That the BHI further to amend the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972. 
be taken into consideration." 
Sir. the Project Tiger has been under implementation since 1973 as a 
scheme of the Government of India. Since then, the Project coverage has also 
increased over the years, from the initial 9 tiger reserves to 28 reserves at 
present. As many as 17 States are involved in the field implementation of the 
Project. 
The Government of India has taken up this project to promote 
conservation of tigers, since the significance of its conservation has 
ramifications beyond State boundaries. Management of forests and wildlife is 
primarily the responsibility of concerned States. Hence, for the field 
implementation of the project, States - which also provide matching grants to 
recurring items of expenditure - deploy field staff/officers and give their 
salaries. The Project Tiger Directorate of the Ministry of Environment and 
Forests is mandated with the task of providing technical guidance and funding 
the project. 
280 

[18 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
The Tiger Reserves are faced with ecological disturbances and 
various other problems. Fragmentation of habitats occur owing to overuse of 
forest habitats, apart from conflicting land uses leading to loss of habitat. Such 
overuse of forest resources distorts the forest dynamics thereby affecting the 
habitat quality to support natural prey base and natal areas for tigers to breed. 
There are also, in some cases, significant resident population in villages 
having many cattle which graze in forests leading to their ecological 
degradation, apart from major sources of regular or intermittent disturbance, 
such as temples and commercial entities such as tea estates. This also leads 
to man-animal conflicts, resulting in tiger and prey mortality. Accordingly, we 
need to strengthen our efforts for the conservation of the species. Several 
constraints affect field implementation of tiger conservation activities. The 
events in the recent past, including, in particular, evidence of large scale 
poaching, have highlighted the fact that there is a need in the States for 
greater commitment and vigilance, apart from strengthening the system at 
Government of India. These concerns can only be effectively addressed by 
providing statutory authority to the Project Tiger by creating the National Tiger 
Conservation Authority, apart from the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau, as 
recommended by the Tiger Task Force appointed by the Prime Minister. The 
Department-Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and 
Technology, Environment and Forests, in its I54 th Report had also strongly 
emphasized the creation of the said Bureau as a statutory body under the 
Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. 
There is no enabling provision in the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 
for constituting a body/authority like Wild Life Crime Control Bureau to take 
measures for preventing and combating wildlife crimes. Hence, there is a 
need for providing an enabling provision in the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. 
These amendments will provide a statutory basis for constituting the "Tiger 
and Other Endangered Species Crime Control Bureau" (Wildlife Crime control 
Bureau) by making enabling provisions. 
Subsequent to giving the amendment notice relating to the Wild Life 
(Protection) Amendment Bill, 2005 pending in this House, the Ministry of 
Environment and Forests had received some suggestions for making some 
modifications in the pending BilI to remove the apprehensions of the tribal 
people living in and around of the tiger reserves. Though the provisions 
contained in the B ill adequately protect such inte rests, a few changes have 
been made in some of the provisions of the Bill. 
281

1.00 PM. 
The proposed amendment would address the ecological as well as 
the administrative concerns for conserving tigers, by creating the Naitonal 
Tiger Conservation Authority, which would provide a statutory basis for 
protection of tiger reserves, apart from ensuring protection of wildlife through 
the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau. It would also address the livelihood 
concerns as well as man-wild animal conflicts in the fringe areas of tiger 
reserves. 
Sir, with these words, I commend the Bill to the House for 
consideration and passing. Now, I seek the suggestions of the hon. Members 
and thereafter I would reply.

both timely and appropriate. I would like to compliment the Ministry of 
Environment and Forests and the hon. Minister for introducing this Bill, which

over the dwindling population of the Tigers. The Sariska experience has been 
none too good in the context of conservation and preservation and there are 
other locations also where such things could be happening on which we do 
not have the full information. So, the entire Bill envisages these things that it 
shall not repeat and we strengthen those of the mechanisms that are critical 
for both preservation and conservation. As Dr. Karan Singh mentioned, 
hundred years ago we had something like a hundred thousand tigers in the 
world. Today, it has dwindled by almost an order of magnitude. I think, it is 
something like 8000 tigers all over the world. Of course, one need not seek too 
far the reasons for this. There is, of course, the question of poaching, the 
habitation laws and, ultimately, of course, the population fragmentation. In all 
these kind of things, particularly if one looks at the habitation laws you have 
the problem of population increase, resettlement, agricultural activities, and 
deforestation. These all add up to the problems related to the tiger number 
dwindling. So, it is against this background that, of course, India had taken 
some very pioneering and visionary steps and the hon. Member Dr. Karan 
Singh himself shared his own experience of pioneering this activity as a part of 
conservation planning way back in 1972.   A Task Force under his

Need to start vocational courses in Schools 
SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY (Andhra Pradesh): Mr. 
Deputy Chairman, Sir, one of the reasons for the dropout of the children, 
especially, in the rural areas is the perception of some parents belonging to 
weaker sections that formal education does not lead to livelihood 
opportunities. Therefore, there is a high dropout rate from age 12 onwards. 
The school dropouts belonging to the weaker sections are being sent by their 
parents to places where they could pick up skills while earning wages. 
Therefore, it is imperative that children are given vocational skills when they 
are in the school, especially, in the higher classes. The present curriculum or 
courses of vocational education are outdated and do not give adequate 
hands-on experience to the students studying in higher classes. The number 
of skills in which training has to be provided has to be increased so as to make 
vocational education more meaningful and relevant to the students in the 
schools in rural areas, where many parents would like their children to support 
them with some immediate employment in view of their poverty. Therefore, 
higher investments for creating infrastructure, appointment of teachers and 
recurring costs, are necessary to achieve this objective in the High Schools. 
Therefore, a secondary education mission may be launched alongwith 
substantial investments. 
Concern over alarming scenario of water contamination and shortage 
DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA (Rajasthan): Sir, in India, the 
problem of water contamination continues to be particularly severe. As many 
as 200 districts across the country suffer from high fluoride concentration in 
the groundwater. The results of the survey conducted by the Fluorosis 
Research and Rural Development Foundation (FRRD) are disturbing, which 
confirmed that groundwater in Delhi's Palam zone was untreated and that over 
35 per cent of children below eight were fluorosis-afflicted. In India, 65 million 
people are estimated to be affected by fluorosis. In Rajasthan, nearly 50 per 
cent of villages are contaminated by fluoride. Apart from fluoride, arsenic 
affects nearly 15 million people in West Bengal. Varying levels of iron 
(particularly in the North-East) and heavy metals like lead, nickel, chromium, 
zinc, copper and manganese, besides nitrates and bacteriological 
contamination in ground water, all serve as slow poison. 
In India, per capita availability which was about 6000 cubic meters 
per annum in 1947, has now come down to about 1,700 cubic meter per 
301 

RAJYA SABHA [18 August, 2006] 
annum in 2002, and will further reduce to 1,340 cubic meters by 2025. This is 
an alarming scenario. However, in a large part of the country's Western and 
Southern region, availability has already reached a 'water-stress' situation of 
less than 1000 cubic meters per capita per annum. Things can only worsen, 
given that India is heading towards a freshwater crisis due to improper 
management of its water resources. No legislation or traditional water 
harvesting system would help resolve freshwater crisis unless conservation 
activities -- from water extraction to water management -- are integrated and 
communities educated. It is time the Government implemented effective 
groundwater legislation on war-footing and encouraged self-regulation by 
communities and local institutions.   Thank you.

THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ): 
Hon. Deputy Chairman, Sir, this is a very important issue which was raised by 
my friend, Shri V. Narayanasamy, by way of a Private Members' Resolution. As 
a matter of fact, this House is aware that two laws were passed -- one was the 
Constitution (Eighty-fourth Amendment) Act, 2001, and the other was 
Delimitation Act, 2002; and, pursuant to these two enactments, a Commission 
was set up, headed by Justice Kuldip Singh along with other Members who 
were associated, according to the scheme of the law.   After that, Members are 
aware that the Election Commission has 
324 

[18 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
gone at a very rapid speed. They have completed the task in Goa, Kerala, 
Tripura, Mizoram, Rajasthan, West Bengal, Punjab, the Union Territory of 
Pondicherry, and they are also at an advanced stage of the work in the States 
of Chhattisgarh, Himachal Pradesh, Orissa, Punjab, Sikkim and the National 
Capital Territory of Delhi. It will be thus seen that the Delimitation Commission's 
work is in full swing and the Commission is a creation of a statute which was 
passed by both Houses of Parliament almost unanimously. But during the 
course of this work, several people have represented about their difficulties. As 
a matter of fact, it is not a regular delimitation, according to my understanding 
of matters, because delimitation, according to the Constitution, is not taking 
place because we have frozen the seats of both the Lok Sabha as well as in 
the Assembly up to 2025 or so. You cannot increase the number of seats but, 
yet, you are dividing the total number of seats with the population of the State 
so that they can be rationalised. Each Parliamentary constituency or Assembly 
onstituency should, as far as possible, have equal number of voters. Then, 
there is a rotation of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribe seats. 
These are two things that are being attempted to. But even during this attempt, 
as you must have noticed, there are a lot of difficulties which are being faced 
particularly in smaller States, North-Eastern States, 
[THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI DINESH TRIVEDI) in the Chair] 
particularly, where tribal population are up in arms. We must maintain the 
prestige of all tribes and give them, at least, one seat each; so, they must get it, 
in order,to protect the tribal culture. Secondly, in smaller States, there is a 
problem of the people settled in the hill States and then in the plains. There is 
another problem which has been brought to my notice, particularly, from 
Karnataka and Maharashtra that urban seats have increased, but rural seats 
have decreased. These representations have been received through our hon. 
Members of Parliament. The Chief Ministers have also spoken to me. I have 
already taken up these issues with the Delimitation Commission and it has 
promised to look into it. Similarly, ail other matters of North-East, Sikkim, 
Mizoram and all smaller States have been taken up with the Delimitation 
Commission. But you must appreciate one basic difficulty that the Delimitation 
Commission is bound by cert ain criteria which are enumerated in the laws 
which were passed by both Houses of Parliament, and there is not much room 
for it to deviate from the norms. So, a consultation process is going on 
nowadays, with all political parties as to whether we can change the guidelines, 
so that all these

null and void and striking down the same unless declared so unanimously by

SHRI SHANTARAM LAXMAN NAIK (Goa): Sir, I beg to move: 
That this House resolves that no legislation passed by the Parliament 
shall be declared as null and void and struck down by the Supreme Court of 
India or any High Court except by a decision unanimously declared so, by a 
bench comprising not less than seven Judges in case of the Supreme Court 
and not less than five Judges in case of the High Courts. 
Sir, I am fortunate enough. There was no match-fixing nor I have 
managed any absentees. I consider that I am fortunate enough to get an 
opportunity for moving this important Resolution.

respect to the judiciary that today, due to various circumstances, the power of 
Parliament to legislate has gone down considerably. If you see, in terms of 
volume, in ordinary terms -- in visual sense I would say - kindly see the 
volume of law that we have enacted and the volume of law which contains in 
various decisions of the courts. In fact, courts are supposed to interpret the 
laws passed by Parliament and in the process of interpretation, the law 
declared by the Supreme Court becomes a law. That is our Constitutional 
position. In the process of interpretation, that is, while interpreting a law, the 
courts can say that this is the meaning of what has been passed by 
Parliament, that is, courts have to explain the meaning of the law passed by
